region: Northern temperate regions of Europe, Asia and North America
description: True poplars, aspens and cottonwoods give a light, soft, pale hardwood used for shelving, boxes, pallets, matches, plywood cores and wood wool, and aspen is used for sauna benches. In North America, 'poplar' lumber is often tulip poplar, which is a different tree (see related species note).

hazards.summary: UK HSE lists sneezing among the reported effects of poplar dust.
UK HSE lists eye irritation from poplar dust.
UK HSE notes that poplar may cause blisters on the skin.

Patch testing has confirmed allergic contact dermatitis to European aspen wood dust and bark, linked to salicyl alcohol and salicylaldehyde in the bark. A Finnish clinic series also recorded a worker with aspen-related dermatitis.
IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancer of the nasal cavity and sinuses after long, heavy exposure. This applies to this wood like any other.

exposure_limits.note: 8-hour TWA; ACGIH value as restated by OSHA.

related_species_note: Tulip poplar or yellow poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera, family Magnoliaceae) is not a Populus and has its own evidence; allergic contact dermatitis to tulip poplar wood and bark has been reported (Wenk-2012). Do not apply this page to tulip poplar. Skin evidence here is from European aspen (Populus tremula).

notes_internal: HSE-WIS30 'Poplar' row (sneezing, eye irritation, may cause blisters) does not name a species. AaltoKorte-2005 case was an elk researcher handling leaves/bark, not a woodworker, but patch test to aspen wood dust was positive. Thiede 1975 (PMID 1122768, aspen 'popple' peelers) found no increased hypersensitivity pneumonitis risk; not cited as a hazard. Carosso 1987 (PMID 3814535) lists poplar SPT per Schlunssen-2018, but the abstract does not name species; not cited. Wenk-2012 is defined only to support the tulip poplar note.
